# Biomass_genericDisturbance

:::{.rmdnote}
This module applies **your** disturbance function at the right moment in a simulation. It
contains no disturbance science of its own.
:::

## What this module is for

In a landscape simulation, disturbances usually arrive in two stages. One module works out
*where and when* something happened — which stands were harvested, which pixels burned,
where an insect outbreak spread. A second step then works out *what that does to the
forest* — which cohorts die, how much biomass is removed, what regenerates.

Historically the second step has been written into a module built for one particular
disturbance, so a new disturbance type means a new module, and the same scheduling and
bookkeeping logic is written again each time.

`Biomass_genericDisturbance` does the second step for **any** disturbance. You tell it, in
your project's global script:

> run function `F` immediately after module `M`'s event `E`

and it schedules `F`, calls it, and adds whatever it returns to the simulation. One
instance of this module can look after every disturbance in a simulation — harvest, fire,
insects, thermokarst — because none of them is built into it.

:::{.rmdimportant}
**The science stays yours.** This module decides *when* your function runs and *what
happens to its results*. It has no opinion about what a disturbance does. If your function
is wrong about the ecology, this module will faithfully run it anyway.
:::

### A note on the name

The `Biomass_` prefix shows the company this module usually keeps — the `Biomass_*` suite
of LandR modules.

## Packages this module installs

The module's own machinery needs only `SpaDES.core` and `data.table`. It also lists
**`LandR`** and **`disturbanceMgmt`** as required packages, so that the disturbance
functions people most often reach for are installed and ready to name in a specification:

- `LandR` provides `FireDisturbance()`, `FireDisturbancePM()` and `PeatlandThermokarst()`.
- `disturbanceMgmt` provides `processPartialDist()` and `plantCohorts()`, for partial
  disturbances such as harvest.

**The module never calls either package.** Nothing in its code refers to them, and it
works just as well with functions of your own, or from any other package. They are listed
for convenience, not because the module depends on them — so if you supply only your own
functions, these two will still be installed but never used.

## Quick start

A single disturbance, applied after a harvest planning module:

```r
simInit(
  modules = list("myHarvestModule", "Biomass_genericDisturbance"),
  params = list(
    Biomass_genericDisturbance = list(
      disturbances = list(
        list(
          fn         = myHarvestEffectFunction,
          name       = "harvestDist",
          after      = "myHarvestModule",
          afterEvent = "harvest",
          triggerObj = "rstCurrentHarvest"
        )
      )
    )
  )
)
```

Two disturbances, each following its own module, in one simulation:

```r
disturbances = list(
  list(fn = myHarvestEffectFunction, name = "harvestDist",
       after = "myHarvestModule", afterEvent = "harvest",
       triggerObj = "rstCurrentHarvest"),
  list(fn = myFireEffectFunction, name = "fireDist",
       after = "myFireModule", afterEvent = "burn",
       triggerObj = "rstCurrentBurn")
)
```

Adding a third disturbance type is another entry in this list. Nothing inside the module
changes, and the existing entries are unaffected.

## The `disturbances` parameter

This parameter is the module's real interface. Each element of the list describes one
disturbance.

| Field | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fn` | yes | — | The function to run. Either a function object, or a character string naming one, e.g. `"LandR::FireDisturbance"`. |
| `name` | yes | — | A unique name for this disturbance. Used as the event name and in all messages. |
| `after` | yes | — | The name of the module to follow. |
| `afterEvent` | yes | — | Which of that module's events to follow. |
| `offset` | no | `0.1` | How closely to follow the upstream event. See "Ordering" below. |
| `triggerObj` | no | `NULL` | The name of a simulation object that must exist and be non-empty for the function to be called. When `NULL`, the function runs every time the upstream event does. |
| `returnsAs` | no | `NULL` | The object name to store the result under, when the function returns a single object rather than a named list. |
| `args` | no | `list()` | Extra arguments passed to the function. These take precedence over simulation objects of the same name. |
| `loopOver` | no | `NULL` | The name of a simulation object holding a list, to call the function once per element of. See "Looping" below. |
| `loopArg` | no | `NULL` | Which function argument receives each element of that list. |
| `loopNameArg` | no | `NULL` | Which function argument receives each element's *name*. |
| `argsFn` | no | `NULL` | A function that builds further arguments for each call, when an argument must be assembled from the current element rather than passed straight through. |

`afterEvent` is required rather than optional because a planning module usually schedules
several events — a `harvest` event, a `plot` event, an end-of-run summary. "After the
module" would be ambiguous; "after the module's `harvest` event" is not.

## Looping over a list of disturbance layers

Planning modules often produce not one disturbance layer but a **named list** of them —
commonly one raster per species. The matching disturbance function usually handles a
single layer at a time, so it has to be called once per element, with each call acting on
the results of the one before.

Set `loopOver` to the name of the list, and the module runs that loop for you:

```r
list(
  fn         = disturbanceMgmt::processPartialDist,
  name       = "harvestDist",
  after      = "simpleHarvestPlanning",
  afterEvent = "harvest",
  triggerObj = "rstCurrentHarvest",

  loopOver   = "speciesHarvestMaps",   # the list, one raster per species
  loopArg    = "partialDistLoc",       # each raster goes to this argument

  ## `partialDistTable` isn't in the simList: it has to be built for each species
  ## from that element's name and the current year.
  argsFn = function(item, itemName, currentTime, sim) {
    list(partialDistTable = data.table::data.table(speciesCode = itemName,
                                                   distYear    = currentTime))
  }
)
```

Each call is given the simulation **as the previous call left it**, so changes accumulate
across species rather than each call overwriting the last one's work. With a list of two
species, the function runs twice per timestep, and the second call sees the `cohortData`
produced by the first.

### Which of the three loop fields to use

- **`loopArg`** — the element itself is an argument. The usual case: each raster goes
  straight to the function's `partialDistLoc` (or equivalent) argument.
- **`loopNameArg`** — the element's *name* is an argument, for a function that takes a
  species code directly. Requires every element of the list to be named.
- **`argsFn`** — an argument has to be **built** from the element. In the example above,
  `processPartialDist()` wants a `partialDistTable` with `speciesCode` and `distYear`
  columns; no such object exists in the simulation, so it is assembled per species. The
  function is given `item`, `itemName`, `currentTime` and `sim`, and must return a named
  list of arguments.

Use any combination. At least one is required when `loopOver` is set, since looping
without passing the element would call the function repeatedly with identical arguments —
the module stops rather than let that happen.

:::{.rmdnote}
**Supplying several inputs to one function** does not require looping. Arguments are
matched to simulation objects by name automatically, so a function taking `cohortData`,
`pixelGroupMap` and `species` receives all three. Use `args` for anything constant that
isn't in the simulation, and `argsFn` for anything that must be computed per call.
:::

### Where the list comes from

`loopOver` names a simulation object, so the list can come from the upstream module (as
`speciesHarvestMaps` does), from another module, or from your global script via
`simInit(objects = ...)`. The module does not care which.

If the named list is empty or missing at a given timestep, the disturbance is skipped with
a message rather than treated as an error — an empty list of harvest maps is a normal
"nothing happened this year". A `loopOver` naming an object that is *never* in the
simulation is an error.

## What your function must look like

Two shapes of function are supported. The module tells them apart by whether the function
has an argument called `sim`.

### Named arguments (recommended for new functions)

Your function takes ordinary named arguments and returns a named list:

```r
myDisturbanceFunction <- function(cohortData, pixelGroupMap, currentTime) {
  ## ... your science here ...
  list(cohortData = cohortData, pixelGroupMap = pixelGroupMap)
}
```

The module fills in the arguments by **matching their names to simulation objects**: an
argument called `cohortData` receives `sim$cohortData`. An argument called `currentTime`
receives the current simulation time. Anything listed in the specification's `args` wins
over both. Anything that cannot be matched is left to your function's own default.

Each element of the returned list is stored in the simulation **under its own name**, so
returning `list(cohortData = ...)` replaces `sim$cohortData`.

If your function returns a single object rather than a list, give the specification a
`returnsAs` field saying what to call it.

:::{.rmdcaution}
**Defaults written in terms of `sim` will not work.** A function whose argument default is
something like `cohortData = copy(sim$cohortData)` cannot be called by this module unless
that argument is matched by name, because `sim` does not exist where the default would be
evaluated. In practice the module matches every argument it can find by name, so such
functions normally work — but do not *rely* on the default being evaluated.
:::

### Taking and returning the simulation

For compatibility with functions already written in the older style, a function whose
first argument is `sim` is simply handed the whole simulation and expected to return it:

```r
myDisturbanceFunction <- function(sim) {
  sim$cohortData <- ...
  invisible(sim)
}
```

This works, but gives up something worth knowing about: because such a function writes to
the simulation itself, **the module cannot report which objects it changed**. With the
named-argument style, every object written is reported in the log. With this style, the
log can only record that the function ran. Prefer named arguments for new functions.

## Ordering: how "immediately after" works

SpaDES has no way to say "run this module after that one". The event queue is sorted by
**time**, and then by **priority** — a number where *lower runs first*. Module identity
plays no part.

So this module works out the priority for you. Each time a disturbance runs, it looks up
when the upstream event is next scheduled and at what priority, and schedules itself at
the same time, at that priority plus `offset` (0.1 by default). If your harvest event runs
at priority 5, the disturbance runs at 5.1 — after harvest, and before anything at 6.

Two consequences worth understanding:

- **The cadence is inherited, not assumed.** The module does not assume disturbances are
  annual. It looks up the upstream event's *next* occurrence each time, so a fire module
  that runs every three years gets a disturbance every three years, and an irregular
  schedule is followed exactly.
- **Disturbances do not interfere with each other.** Each one sits just below its own
  upstream event, so they occupy different parts of the ordering. Adding a disturbance
  never changes when the others run.

### The first timestep

At the moment this module starts up, the other modules may not have scheduled anything
yet, so there is nothing to follow. The module therefore runs a one-off `bootstrap` event
at the very end of the first timestep, once every module has started, and works out each
disturbance's schedule from there. If an upstream event has *already run* in that first
timestep, its disturbance is scheduled immediately so the first timestep is not skipped.

If a module is present but has not yet scheduled the event you named — because it starts
later in the simulation — the module waits and checks again next year, reporting that it
has done so.

## When the module stops the simulation

Several mistakes would otherwise produce a simulation that runs to completion and gives
plausible but wrong answers. Those are treated as errors rather than warnings, because a
warning is easy to miss in a long batch run:

- The module named in `after` has no events at all — usually a misspelling, or a module
  left out of the simulation.
- Two disturbances would run at exactly the same time and priority, which would make their
  order depend on module load order rather than on anything you specified.
- A disturbance is about to run while the event it follows is still waiting to run.
- `offset` is zero or negative, which would place the disturbance before the event it
  follows.
- A function returns a list with unnamed elements, or a single object with no `returnsAs`
  to name it.
- A `sim`-style function returns something that is not the simulation.
- The simulation's time unit is not `"year"` (see "Limitations").

## Limitations

These are real constraints, not oversights. Read them before relying on the module.

**It declares no inputs or outputs.** Look at this module's metadata and you will find
`inputObjects` and `outputObjects` empty. That is deliberate: what the module reads and
writes depends entirely on the functions you supply, and cannot be known in advance.

The consequence is that **a downstream module cannot declare `expectsInput()` on anything
this module produces**, because nothing declares that it is produced. If one of your
disturbance functions creates an object that another module needs — a carbon flux, say —
that dependency is real but invisible to SpaDES, and nothing will warn you if it breaks.
The messages this module prints as it runs are the only record of what it wrote, which is
why `verboseDisturbance` defaults to `TRUE`.

**Anything your function returns will overwrite what is already there.** That is the point
when it returns `cohortData`. But the same applies to a name you did not intend: a typo in
a returned list's names will quietly replace an unrelated simulation object. The module
cannot tell the difference, because it does not know what the names mean. Every write is
reported in the log, so the damage is visible — but it is not prevented.

**Ordering is checked; freshness is not.** The `triggerObj` check catches an object that is
missing or empty. It cannot tell an object written in this timestep from one left over
from a previous one. If an upstream module fails to update its output, the disturbance
will be applied to stale information without complaint.

**The simulation must use annual time.** The module reads event times from the queue and
passes them back when scheduling, and these are interpreted in different units in the two
places. They agree when everything is annual. Rather than convert — where a mistake would
silently shift disturbances into the wrong years — the module stops if the simulation's
time unit is not `"year"`.

**Caching is not appropriate here.** Disturbances are typically stochastic, so caching this
module's events would replay an old disturbance instead of generating a new one.
`.useCache` defaults to `FALSE` and should normally stay that way.

## Parameters

```{r moduleParams, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
df_params <- SpaDES.core::moduleParams("Biomass_genericDisturbance", "..")
knitr::kable(df_params)
```

## Input objects

None declared. See "Limitations" above: the objects read depend on the functions supplied
through the `disturbances` parameter, and are validated when the simulation starts rather
than by `simInit()`.

## Output objects

None declared, for the same reason. The module writes whatever the supplied functions
return, and reports each object it writes.

## Links to other modules

This module is designed to follow any module that produces disturbance information. It has
no required companions and no dependencies on other modules.
